definition: 7-layer reference model: Physical, Data Link, Network, Transport, Session, Presentation, Application. Mnemonic: Please Do Not Throw Sausage Pizza Away.
Connection-oriented Layer 4 protocol. Uses 3-way handshake (SYN, SYN-ACK, ACK). Guarantees delivery via acknowledgements and retransmission.
Connectionless Layer 4 protocol. No handshake, no guaranteed delivery. Used for DNS, DHCP, VoIP, streaming — where speed > reliability.
Layer 3 connectionless protocol responsible for logical addressing and routing packets between networks. IPv4 (32-bit) and IPv6 (128-bit).
Application layer protocol for web traffic. Port 80. Cleartext — all data visible in transit. Replaced by HTTPS for secure communication.
HTTP over TLS/SSL. Port 443. Encrypts web traffic using certificates. Standard for all modern web communication.
Ports 20 (data) and 21 (control). Cleartext file transfer. Active mode: server initiates data connection back to client. Passive mode: client initiates both connections.
Secure file transfer over SSH. Port 22. Encrypts both commands and data. Replaces FTP and FTPS for secure file transfers.
FTP over SSL/TLS. Uses ports 989/990. Different from SFTP (which uses SSH/port 22). Adds encryption to standard FTP.
Port 22. Encrypted remote CLI access. Replaces Telnet. Uses asymmetric encryption for key exchange, symmetric for session. Also tunnels SFTP and SCP.
Port 25 (server-to-server), 587 (submission with auth). Sends email outbound. Does not retrieve email — use POP3 or IMAP for that.
Port 53 (UDP for queries, TCP for zone transfers). Resolves hostnames to IP addresses. NXDOMAIN = name doesn't exist. Poisoning mitigated by DNSSEC.
Ports 67 (server) / 68 (client). UDP. Assigns IP, subnet mask, gateway, DNS via DORA (Discover, Offer, Request, Acknowledge). Option 3 = gateway, Option 6 = DNS.
Port 69. UDP. Stripped-down FTP with no authentication. Used for network booting (PXE), IOS image transfers, config backups on trusted networks.
Port 110 (995 for SSL). Downloads email from server to client and typically deletes from server. Single-device access. IMAP preferred for multi-device.
Port 143 (993 for SSL). Keeps email on server, syncs across multiple devices. Better than POP3 for modern multi-device access.
Port 161 (polling) / 162 (traps). UDP. Monitors network devices. v1/v2c use cleartext community strings. v3 adds authentication and AES encryption (AuthPriv). MIB stores OIDs.
Port 389. Used to query and modify directory services (Active Directory). Cleartext. LDAPS (port 636) adds SSL/TLS encryption.
Port 445. Windows file and printer sharing protocol. SMBv1 vulnerable to EternalBlue/WannaCry. Disable SMBv1, use v2/v3.
Port 3389. TCP. Microsoft remote desktop access. High-value attack target — restrict with firewall rules, use MFA, avoid exposing to internet.
Port 123. UDP. Synchronizes clocks across network devices. Critical for Kerberos auth — clock skew > 5 min breaks AD authentication. Uses stratum levels.
Port 179. TCP. Exterior Gateway Protocol (EGP) — routes between autonomous systems on the internet. Path-vector protocol. AD = 20 (eBGP), 200 (iBGP).
Ports 5060 (UDP/TCP) / 5061 (TLS). Sets up, manages, and tears down VoIP and multimedia sessions. Signaling only — RTP carries the actual audio.
UDP ports 16384–32767 (typically). Carries actual voice/video data in VoIP. Works with SIP. Requires QoS: latency <150ms, jitter <30ms, packet loss <1%.
Link-state routing protocol. AD = 110. Uses Dijkstra's SPF algorithm. Scales with areas (Area 0 = backbone). Multicast 224.0.0.5/224.0.0.6. Classless, fast convergence.
Cisco hybrid (distance-vector + link-state) routing protocol. AD = 90 (internal), 170 (external). Uses DUAL algorithm. Classless, fast convergence, multicast 224.0.0.10.
Distance-vector routing protocol. AD = 120. Max 15 hops (16 = unreachable). Slow convergence. RIPv2 supports CIDR and authentication. Largely obsolete.
Translates private IP addresses to public. Types: Static (1-to-1), Dynamic (pool), PAT/Overloaded (many-to-1 using ports). Extends IPv4 address space.
NAT overload — maps many private IPs to one public IP using unique source port numbers. Most common home/small office setup. Also called NAT overloading.
Category of protocols providing redundant default gateways. Includes HSRP (Cisco), VRRP (open standard), and GLBP (Cisco, load balancing). Virtual IP shared between routers.
Cisco proprietary FHRP. Active/Standby model — only Active forwards traffic. UDP 1985. Virtual IP and MAC shared. Higher priority = Active. Preemption optional.
Open-standard FHRP (RFC 5798). Master/Backup model. IP protocol 112. Highest priority = Master. Preemption enabled by default. Non-Cisco alternative to HSRP.
Cisco proprietary FHRP. Active Virtual Gateway (AVG) assigns virtual MACs to Active Virtual Forwarders (AVFs). True load balancing across multiple gateways simultaneously.
IEEE 802.1D. Prevents Layer 2 loops by blocking redundant paths. States: Blocking → Listening → Learning → Forwarding (30-50 sec). Root bridge = lowest Bridge ID.
IEEE 802.1w. Converges in <1 second vs STP's 30-50 sec. Backward compatible with STP. Uses Discarding/Learning/Forwarding states. Edge ports (PortFast equivalent) immediate forwarding.
Logical segmentation of a switch at Layer 2. Isolates broadcast domains without physical separation. Tagged with 802.1Q on trunk ports. Native VLAN = untagged on trunk.
Cisco proprietary — propagates VLAN database across switches. Modes: Server, Client, Transparent. Dangerous: a new server with higher revision number can wipe all VLANs. Often disabled.
Cisco proprietary — auto-negotiates trunk links between switches. Security risk: attackers can send DTP frames to become a trunk (VLAN hopping). Best practice: disable DTP, set ports manually.

IEEE 802.3ad. Bundles multiple physical links into one logical EtherChannel. Modes: Active (sends LACP) / Passive (waits). Active+Active or Active+Passive = channel forms. Passive+Passive = no channel.
IEEE 802.1AB. Open-standard Layer 2 neighbor discovery. Devices advertise identity, capabilities, and neighbors. Vendor-neutral alternative to Cisco's CDP.
Cisco proprietary Layer 2 neighbor discovery. Advertises device type, IOS version, IP, port, capabilities. Security risk: disable on untrusted ports as it reveals device info.
Resolves IP addresses to MAC addresses on a local network. Broadcast request, unicast reply. ARP cache stores mappings. Vulnerable to ARP poisoning — mitigated by DAI.
48-bit Layer 2 hardware address burned into NIC (BIA). Format: XX:XX:XX:XX:XX:XX. First 3 octets = OUI (manufacturer). Used for local delivery within a network segment.
Wireless network name broadcast by an AP. Hiding SSID provides minimal security (still discoverable via probe requests). Up to 32 characters. BSSID = AP's MAC address.
IEEE 802.11i. Personal (PSK) or Enterprise (802.1X/RADIUS). Uses AES-CCMP encryption. Vulnerable to PMKID/dictionary attacks on PSK. Superseded by WPA3 but still widely deployed.
Latest Wi-Fi security standard. Replaces PSK with SAE (Simultaneous Authentication of Equals) — protects against offline dictionary attacks. Mandatory for Wi-Fi 6 (802.11ax) devices.
WPA3 replacement for PSK. Dragonfly key exchange — provides forward secrecy and protects against offline brute-force attacks even if attacker captures the handshake.
WPA1 encryption — RC4 with per-packet key mixing. Deprecated and broken. Never use. WPA2 with AES-CCMP is minimum; WPA3 preferred.

full_name: Counter Mode with Cipher Block Chaining Message Authentication Code Protocol
definition: Encryption protocol used in WPA2. Based on AES-128. Provides both confidentiality and integrity. Replaced TKIP. Required for WPA2 certification.

full_name: Control And Provisioning of Wireless Access Points
definition: Protocol between lightweight APs (LWAP) and Wireless LAN Controllers (WLC). UDP 5246 (control) / 5247 (data). LWAP tunnels all traffic to WLC for central management.
Centralized controller for lightweight APs (LWAP) in enterprise Wi-Fi. Manages config, roaming, RF, security policy via CAPWAP. APs are thin — all intelligence at WLC.
Notation for representing IP addresses with variable-length subnet masks (e.g., 192.168.1.0/24). Replaced classful addressing. Enables route summarization and efficient IP allocation.
Range 169.254.0.0/16. Self-assigned when DHCP fails. Indicates DHCP server unreachable or scope exhausted. Only provides local link connectivity — no routing.
IPv6 mechanism for self-configuration without DHCPv6. Client uses router advertisement (RA) prefix + EUI-64 (derived from MAC) or random suffix. RFC 4862.
EUI-64: 64-bit interface ID used in IPv6 SLAAC, derived from 48-bit MAC by inserting FFFE in the middle and flipping the universal/local bit.
Largest Layer 3 packet size a link can carry. Ethernet default = 1500 bytes. Jumbo frames = 9000 bytes. MTU mismatch causes fragmentation or black-holing with PMTUD.
IP header field decremented by 1 at each router hop. Prevents infinite routing loops. Packet dropped (ICMP Time Exceeded sent) when TTL = 0. Used by traceroute.
Mechanisms to prioritize traffic types. VoIP needs: latency <150ms, jitter <30ms, loss <1%. Tools: DSCP marking, CoS, LLQ (strict priority), shaping, policing.
6-bit field in IP header for Layer 3 QoS marking. EF (Expedited Forwarding) = 46 for VoIP. BE (Best Effort) = 0 default. Enables per-hop behavior (PHB) at each router.
3-bit PCP field in 802.1Q VLAN tag (values 0-7). Layer 2 QoS marking. Lost when traffic leaves the VLAN trunk — must map to DSCP for end-to-end QoS.
Ordered list of permit/deny rules. Standard ACL: source IP only, place near destination. Extended ACL: source+dest+port+protocol, place near source. Implicit deny all at end.
Passive — monitors copy of traffic (SPAN/TAP), alerts on threats but cannot block. Signature-based (known threats) or anomaly-based (behavioral). Generates alerts for SOC review.
Inline — sits in traffic path, can block/drop malicious traffic in real time. Adds latency. False positives drop legitimate traffic. Can be signature or anomaly-based.
Deep packet inspection beyond port/protocol. Features: App-ID (application awareness), user identity, SSL inspection, IPS, threat intelligence feeds. Examples: Palo Alto, Fortinet.
Filters HTTP/HTTPS traffic, protects web apps against OWASP Top 10 (SQLi, XSS, CSRF). Sits in front of web server. Application-layer protection standard firewall can't provide.
All-in-one security appliance combining firewall, IPS, antivirus, URL filtering, VPN, DLP. Simpler management for SMBs but single point of failure. Replaced by NGFW in enterprise.
Network segment between two firewalls hosting public-facing servers (web, email, DNS). Internet can reach DMZ. DMZ cannot initiate connections to internal network. Defense in depth.
Encrypted tunnel over public network. Types: Site-to-site (IPsec, connects networks), Remote access (SSL/TLS port 443 or IPsec). Split tunneling: only corp traffic through VPN.
Suite for encrypting/authenticating IP traffic. Protocols: ESP (50, encrypt+auth) and AH (51, auth only). Modes: Transport (host-to-host) and Tunnel (network-to-network). Uses IKE for key exchange.
IPsec key negotiation. Phase 1: ISAKMP SA (management tunnel, DH key exchange). Phase 2: IPsec SA (data tunnel). UDP 500 (IKE), UDP 4500 (NAT-T). IKEv2 is current standard.
IPsec protocol 50. Provides encryption, authentication, and anti-replay. Can be used alone (preferred) — encrypts payload and authenticates. Used in both Transport and Tunnel modes.
IPsec protocol 51. Authentication and integrity only — no encryption. Incompatible with NAT (covers IP headers). Rarely used alone; ESP preferred. Provides anti-replay protection.
Predecessor to TLS. All versions (1.0, 2.0, 3.0) are deprecated and broken (POODLE, DROWN). Must not be used. TLS 1.2+ required; TLS 1.3 preferred.
Successor to SSL. TLS 1.2 minimum; TLS 1.3 preferred. Used by HTTPS (443), SMTPS, LDAPS, etc. Handshake negotiates cipher suite; asymmetric for key exchange, symmetric for data.
System for managing digital certificates and asymmetric keys. CA issues/signs certificates. CRL lists revoked certs. OCSP provides real-time per-cert revocation check.
Trusted entity that signs and issues digital certificates. Root CA → Intermediate CA → End-entity cert (chain of trust). Self-signed certs have no trusted CA — browsers warn users.
List of certificates revoked before expiry. Published by CA. Client downloads and checks. Can be stale (published periodically). OCSP is preferred for real-time revocation checking.
Real-time certificate revocation check. Client queries OCSP responder with certificate serial number, gets Good/Revoked/Unknown response. Faster and more current than CRL.
Uses ephemeral DH keys per session. Even if long-term private key is compromised, past sessions remain encrypted. Implemented via DHE or ECDHE cipher suites. Best practice for TLS and IPsec.
Security framework: Authentication (who are you — identity), Authorization (what can you do — permissions), Accounting (what did you do — logging). Implemented via RADIUS or TACACS+.
AAA protocol. UDP 1812 (auth) / 1813 (accounting). Encrypts only password in packet. Used for network access control (Wi-Fi 802.1X, VPN). Open standard.

full_name: Terminal Access Controller Access Control System Plus
definition: Cisco AAA protocol. TCP 49. Encrypts entire payload (not just password). Separates A/A/A functions independently. Used for device administration. More secure and flexible than RADIUS.
Layer 2 security — validates ARP packets against DHCP snooping binding table. Drops ARP replies with MAC/IP pairs not in the binding table. Prevents ARP poisoning/MITM attacks.
Adds digital signatures to DNS records. Validates DNS responses to prevent DNS cache poisoning (Kaminsky attack). Provides data origin authentication and integrity, not confidentiality.
SNMP database structure. Hierarchical tree of OIDs (Object Identifiers) each representing a manageable object on a device (e.g., interface stats, CPU usage). Defined in RFC/vendor MIBs.
Unique numeric path in the SNMP MIB tree identifying a specific managed object. Example: 1.3.6.1.2.1.1.1 = sysDescr. SNMP manager polls OIDs to get device metrics.
IETF standard (RFC 7011) for exporting IP flow data. Successor to Cisco NetFlow v9. Sends flow records to a collector on UDP 4739 (or 2055 for NetFlow compatibility).
Port mirroring — copies traffic from source port(s) or VLAN to a monitor port for analysis (IDS/packet capture). Local to one switch. RSPAN extends mirroring across multiple switches.
Extends SPAN across multiple switches using a dedicated RSPAN VLAN. Traffic mirrored to a remote analyzer port on a different switch. Requires all transit switches to support RSPAN VLAN.
Contract defining minimum service standards. Common metric: uptime percentage. 99.9% = 8.76 hr/yr downtime. 99.99% = 52.6 min/yr. 99.999% (five nines) = 5.26 min/yr.
Maximum acceptable downtime after a disaster — how quickly must systems be restored? Business defines this. Drives DR site type: hot (minutes), warm (hours), cold (days/weeks).
Maximum acceptable data loss measured in time — how old can the recovered data be? RPO of 1hr means backups every hour. Drives backup frequency and replication strategy.
Average time between hardware failures. Higher = more reliable. Used to calculate availability: MTBF / (MTBF + MTTR). Key metric for hardware procurement and HA design.
Average time to restore a failed component. Lower = faster recovery. Availability = MTBF / (MTBF + MTTR). Drives sparing strategy and support contract SLAs.
Disk redundancy/performance technology. RAID 0: no redundancy. RAID 1: mirror. RAID 5: single parity (1 failure). RAID 6: dual parity (2 failures). RAID 10: mirror+stripe. NOT a backup.
Most common LAN cabling. Cat5e (1 Gbps/100m), Cat6 (1 Gbps/100m or 10 Gbps/55m), Cat6A (10 Gbps/100m), Cat8 (40 Gbps/30m). TIA-568: max 90m horizontal + 10m patch = 100m total.
Fiber with larger core (50 or 62.5 micron). Uses LED or VCSEL light source. Shorter distances (up to ~550m at 10G). Less expensive than SMF. OM1/OM2/OM3/OM4/OM5 grades.
Fiber with small core (9 micron). Uses laser light source. Long distances (up to 100km+). Used for WAN/backbone/service provider links. More expensive than MMF. OS1/OS2 grades.
Hot-swappable transceiver module for fiber or copper interfaces. SFP = 1 Gbps. SFP+ = 10 Gbps. QSFP = 40 Gbps. QSFP28 = 100 Gbps. Allows flexible media type selection.
Fiber optic test tool. Sends light pulse, measures reflections to locate breaks, splices, connectors. Measures distance to fault and measures insertion loss. Essential for fiber troubleshooting.
Copper cable test tool. Sends signal pulse, measures reflections to locate opens, shorts, and impedance mismatches. Reports distance to fault. Some cable certifiers include TDR functionality.
IEEE 802.3af (15.4W), 802.3at/PoE+ (30W), 802.3bt/PoE++ (60-100W). Delivers power over UTP to APs, IP phones, cameras. PSE (switch) provides power; PD (device) receives it.
Core network room — primary termination point for building cabling. Houses core switches, routers, servers, and WAN connections. IDFs connect back to MDF via vertical/backbone cabling.
Floor-level wiring closet. Houses access layer switches. Connects to MDF via backbone cabling. Horizontal runs from IDF to workstation outlets max 90m (TIA-568).
Battery backup for power outages. Types: Offline/standby (5-25ms switchover), Line-interactive (AVR, <4ms), Online/Double-conversion (0ms, cleanest power). Sized by VA/watts and runtime.
Tunneling protocol (IP protocol 47). Encapsulates any Layer 3 protocol. No encryption (often combined with IPsec). Used for site-to-site VPN and multicast/routing-over-VPN scenarios.
WAN technology using labels (not IP lookups) for fast packet forwarding. Provider assigns labels at ingress (LER), core routers (LSR) forward by label. Supports VPNs and traffic engineering.
Layer 2 overlay over Layer 3 network. Uses UDP 4789. Extends VLANs across routed networks (data centers, cloud). Supports 16 million VNIs vs 4094 VLAN limit. Used in SDN/overlay networks.
Decouples control plane from data plane. Centralized controller (northbound API to apps, southbound to devices via OpenFlow). Enables programmable, automated network management.
Virtualizes network appliances (firewalls, load balancers, routers) as software on commodity hardware. Reduces physical appliance costs. Often paired with SDN in modern data centers.
Abstracts WAN connectivity — routes traffic across multiple links (MPLS, broadband, LTE) based on policy. Centralized management, application-aware routing, reduced MPLS dependence.
Interface for software components to communicate. REST APIs (HTTP/JSON) used for network automation and SDN. Enables programmatic device configuration vs manual CLI.
IETF publication defining Internet standards and protocols. Normative language: MUST (required), SHOULD (recommended), MAY (optional). Examples: RFC 791 (IPv4), RFC 2460 (IPv6).
Encapsulates PPP frames in Ethernet. Common for DSL broadband connections — ISP authenticates subscriber over PPP using CHAP/PAP. Adds 8-byte overhead, reducing MTU to 1492.
Layer 3 protocol for error reporting and diagnostics. Used by ping (echo request/reply) and traceroute (TTL exceeded). Not for data transfer. ICMP redirect, unreachable, time exceeded messages.
Document defining permitted and prohibited use of company network/systems. Users must acknowledge and sign. Basis for disciplinary action when violated. Covers internet, email, device use.
Policy allowing employees to use personal devices for work. Requires MDM/MAM for policy enforcement, certificate-based auth, NAC to segment personal vs corporate traffic.
Platform for enforcing policies on mobile devices. Can remotely wipe, enforce encryption, require PINs, restrict apps. Key control for BYOD programs. Examples: Intune, JAMF, AirWatch.
Technology/policy preventing sensitive data from leaving the organization. Inspects email, web, USB transfers for PII, credit cards, IP. Alerts or blocks based on content classification rules.
Controls which devices can connect to the network based on posture (patch level, AV status, certificates). Uses 802.1X, RADIUS, and agents to enforce health checks before granting access.
Sophisticated, long-term targeted attack, typically nation-state sponsored. Stealth over speed — establish foothold, maintain persistence, exfiltrate data over months/years. Hard to detect.
Attack overwhelming a target to make it unavailable. Single attacker. Types: volumetric (bandwidth), protocol (SYN flood), application (HTTP flood). DDoS = distributed (botnet).
DoS using many compromised systems (botnet). Categories: Volumetric (DNS amplification), Protocol (SYN flood), Application (HTTP flood). Mitigated by scrubbing centers and rate limiting.
Attacker intercepts communication between two parties. Methods: ARP poisoning, rogue AP, DNS spoofing. Mitigated by encryption (TLS), certificate pinning, DAI, and 802.1X.
Authentication using 2+ factors: something you know (password), something you have (token/phone), something you are (biometric). Significantly reduces credential-based attack success.
Attacker gains access to traffic on other VLANs. Methods: switch spoofing (DTP) or double-tagging (native VLAN). Mitigated by disabling DTP, changing native VLAN to unused VLAN.
Design goal minimizing downtime through redundancy. Components: redundant hardware, failover clustering, load balancing, FHRP. Availability = MTBF / (MTBF + MTTR).
Platform for monitoring and managing network devices. Collects data via SNMP, NetFlow, syslog. Provides dashboards, alerts, trending. Examples: SolarWinds, PRTG, Nagios, Zabbix.
Text-based interface for device management. Used in routers, switches, firewalls. Key commands: show ip route, show interfaces, show vlan, debug, ping, traceroute. Faster than GUI for experts.
DHCP lease process mnemonic. Client broadcasts Discover → server unicasts/broadcasts Offer → client broadcasts Request → server broadcasts Acknowledge. All initial messages use broadcasts.
Translates IPv6 addresses to IPv4 for communication between IPv6-only and IPv4-only networks. Enables IPv6 clients to reach IPv4 servers during IPv4-to-IPv6 transition.
OSPF adapted for IPv6. Uses link-local addresses for neighbor adjacencies. Runs over IPv6. Supports multiple address families. Otherwise same SPF algorithm and area concept as OSPFv2.
PPP authentication method. Three-way handshake using MD5 hash of shared secret. Never sends password in cleartext. Periodically re-authenticates. More secure than PAP.
Simple PPP authentication. Sends username and password in cleartext. Insecure — avoid unless on encrypted link. Superseded by CHAP and EAP.
Authentication framework used with 802.1X. Multiple methods: EAP-TLS (certificate-based, most secure), PEAP (password in TLS tunnel), EAP-TTLS. Transported over RADIUS.
EAP method that creates a TLS tunnel for inner authentication (usually MSCHAPv2). Requires only server-side certificate. Widely used for 802.1X Wi-Fi enterprise authentication.
Router's trust ranking for routing protocol sources. Lower = more trusted. Connected=0, Static=1, eBGP=20, EIGRP=90, OSPF=110, RIP=120, iBGP=200. Used when multiple protocols know same route.
Dijkstra's algorithm used by OSPF to calculate loop-free paths. Each router builds complete topology map (LSDB) and independently calculates shortest path tree to all destinations.
OSPF's topology table — contains all LSAs (Link State Advertisements) collected from all routers in the area. All routers in same area have identical LSDB. SPF runs against LSDB.
Generic term for data at each OSI layer. Layer 7-5: Data, Layer 4: Segment (TCP) / Datagram (UDP), Layer 3: Packet, Layer 2: Frame, Layer 1: Bit/Symbol.
